answer.evidence: The silhouette is a constant 16 px wide from row 1 to row 15, so nothing widens or narrows like an ellipse. At the middle column the light tan row 2 is only a 1-row rail highlight over brown face rows 3-4. At the post columns the light row 0 is a 1-row cap highlight over brown rows 1-2. The rail therefore has at most 2-3 rows, which is a rim and not a top surface. Row 6 is a reddish edge line on the sheet, with a dark row 5 above it. The corrugated sheet (rows 7-14, blue-gray) and the posts (rows 3-14) are drawn as vertical faces only. No horizontal top surface is visible on the rail, the posts or the base. The object reads as a flat front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is about one tile in size. It measures 13 visible tones per 16x16 tile, above the hedge reference (9) and below the stall (17) and well (20). Near-flat coverage is 0%, so there are no 5x5 flat fills, and the corrugation ridges and post grain break up the surfaces. The dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outline is tinted. That matches Beodeul's practice of using the dark tone of the neighbouring material (brown beside wood, dark blue-grey beside metal) rather than a uniform black line. With only 13 colours across the posts and the metal sheet, each material gets roughly 4 steps, a little under Beodeul's 5-6. For a thin, sparse prop like a fence, though, it would sit next to the hedge and bench without looking flatter or more sticker-like. I judged this partly by eye because the candidate is very small on the board, and it passes on the measured facts and the tinted outline.
